claim.pdf_says: D.8.2   Weakly-typed items  /  D.8.3   Strongly-typed group items (both set at the same typographic rank as D.8.1 General on p1091, i.e. third-level subclauses of D.8 Types)
claim.markdown_says: ## D.8.2 Weakly-typed items  /  ## D.8.3 Strongly-typed group items (level 2, while their sibling '### D.8.1 General' is level 3 and their parent '## D.8 Types' is level 2)
claim.why_it_matters: D.8.2 and D.8.3 are promoted to the same heading level as their own parent D.8, and outrank their sibling D.8.1. The generated outline therefore shows D.8.2/D.8.3 as peers of D.8 rather than as its subclauses. The break falls exactly at the page boundary, the signature of the slicing artefact: the first heading on a fresh page is emitted at level 2 regardless of its numbering depth.

verdict.reasoning:
REFUTED on three independent grounds.

(1) Nothing is missing. kind=missing-heading is a misnomer. Rendered E:/Temp/specrecon/v1092/spec_p1092.png at 300 dpi: the page prints 'D.8.2   Weakly-typed items' and 'D.8.3   Strongly-typed group items'. specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 43811 reads '## D.8.2 Weakly-typed items' and line 43840 reads '## D.8.3 Strongly-typed group items'. Both headings are present with the exact clause number and the exact title text. The surrounding body text, both COBOL code blocks (Feature TYPEDEF / Equipment, and the expanded record) and the 49-level sentence all transcribe faithfully. No content is lost.

(2) The claim's premise about the PDF is false. The claim asserts D.8.2/D.8.3 are typographically ranked as third-level subclauses BELOW D.8. I cropped and compared the printed glyphs directly (E:/Temp/specrecon/v1091/crop_d8_d81.png, E:/Temp/specrecon/v1092/crop_d82.png). 'D.8   Types', 'D.8.1   General' and 'D.8.2   Weakly-typed items' are set in the IDENTICAL bold face, at the IDENTICAL point size, flush to the IDENTICAL left margin. ISO gives Annex D headings no typographic rank differentiation at all; depth is carried solely by the dotted clause number. D.8.2 is at the same visual rank as D.8.1 AND as D.8. There is therefore no PDF-side level information for the markdown to have lost, and no basis for calling '### D.8.1' the correct rendering and '## D.8.2' the wrong one.

(3) Heading depth in this transcription is page furniture, not a document outline. The file emits '# ISO/IEC 1989:2023 (E)' at level 1 on 941 pages and '## Page NNNN' at level 2 on 1261 pages; each page slice then restarts clause headings at level 2 and nests relatively within that page (e.g. p1092 gives '## D.8.2' then its sibling '## D.8.3'). This is a global, uniform property of the whole transcription -- 'D.2.2.2', 'D.2.3.2.3', 'D.6.1.2' and dozens more show the same reset -- not a p1092 defect. There is no coherent global outline to corrupt, because the outline is already page-partitioned by construction. Under the reconciliation rules this is page-break furniture and formatting, and it changes no meaning: a reader or tool resolving 'D.8.2' finds the correct clause with the correct text.

Minor additional inaccuracy in the claim: the stated mechanism ('the first heading on a fresh page is emitted at level 2') does not explain D.8.3, which is not the first heading on p1092. D.8.3 is level 2 because it is a sibling of the page's first heading under the per-page relative nesting scheme.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a content discrepancy. Both headings are present verbatim with correct clause numbers and titles, and the entire body of D.8.2 and D.8.3 on this page transcribes faithfully. The PDF sets D.8, D.8.1, D.8.2 and D.8.3 in one identical bold face at one identical size, so the PDF encodes no heading rank for the markdown to lose. The observed '##' level is the transcription's uniform per-page slicing convention (941 level-1 running-header headings, 1261 level-2 'Page NNNN' headings, clause headings restarted at level 2 per page), applying document-wide and not specific to p1092. If the project wants a semantic outline, that is a one-time global post-processing pass driven by the dotted clause numbers -- not a per-page reconciliation finding.
